name: Yangang
tagline: Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali farms below Maenam's Bhaleydhunga
meta_description: Yangang, South Sikkim: Bhaleydhunga rock, Neya Khola falls, Lepcha and Gurung monasteries, village homestays, how to reach and honest 2026 costs.
summary: Yangang is a mixed Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali village at about 1,500 m on the eastern flank of the Maenam ridge, around 45 minutes to an hour from Ravangla. It suits walkers and slow travellers: homestays, three village monasteries, Neya Khola falls and the long trail towards Bhaleydhunga, the great rock on Maenam's ridge.
intro: Yangang spreads across the slope east of Maenam hill, looking down towards the Teesta side of Sikkim rather than the Rangeet. It is a working village of maize, ginger, cardamom and vegetable fields, with Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali families living side by side. The Wikipedia article on the village lists its Lepcha Monastery, Gurung Monastery and Yangang Monastery, a Shiva shrine at Mahadev Than, Neya Khola falls and Tig-Day Cho lake among its sights.

Above it all rises Bhaleydhunga, a huge rock outcrop on the Maenam ridge whose Nepali name is usually translated as rooster rock, for its shape. It is visible from much of South Sikkim and is the goal of a long, steep guided walk from the village. The state has proposed tourism projects around it, including a ropeway and a skywalk; check current status before you travel, as such plans change.

Yangang is also a place of some weight in Sikkim's public life. It is the birthplace of Pawan Kumar Chamling, Chief Minister from 1994 to 2019, the site chosen for Sikkim University's campus and home to the state's main police training centre. None of this shows much on a village walk. What you see are farms, monasteries and homestays where you eat with the family.

story.title: Bhaleydhunga, the rooster rock above the village
story.text: From Yangang, the eye keeps returning to one point on the skyline: a sheer, beak-like outcrop on the Maenam ridge. Its Nepali name, Bhaleydhunga, joins bhale, a rooster, and dhunga, a stone, and the Wikipedia article on Yangang lists it, as Bhalay-Dhunga, at the top of the village's natural sights. As told locally, Lepcha families hold the rock in particular respect and tell stories about it, but we have not found a written source for them, so we leave them for your hosts to tell in their own words. What is documented is the rock's place in plans for the area. The same article notes a proposed ropeway and skywalk to Bhaleydhunga and a Lepcha heritage centre in Yangang, and the Sikkim government has announced such projects at various times. Until anything is built, the only way up is on foot: a long, steep walk through the forests of the Maenam ridge with a local guide, starting before dawn and returning in the afternoon.

little_known.fact: Yangang is the birthplace of Pawan Kumar Chamling, who was Chief Minister of Sikkim from 1994 to 2019, a tenure of nearly 25 years.
little_known.source: Wikipedia: Yangang; Wikipedia: Pawan Kumar Chamling

little_known.fact: Yangang was chosen as the site of Sikkim University's permanent campus, and the state's largest police training centre is also located in the village.
Yangang has both a Lepcha monastery and a Gurung monastery, a sign of the village's mixed communities, alongside the main Yangang Monastery.

facts: ≈ 1,500 m (Bhaleydhunga far higher, on the Maenam ridge)

highlights.title: Bhaleydhunga from below and above
highlights.text: The rooster-shaped rock on the Maenam ridge dominates Yangang's skyline. Most visitors admire it from the village; fit walkers can make a long, steep guided day hike through the forest towards it. Start before dawn, carry food and water, and go only in dry weather.

highlights.title: Neya Khola falls
highlights.text: A forest stream and waterfall close to the village, at its fullest just after the monsoon in September and October. A short walk with your host makes a good first outing. Paths are slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip.

highlights.title: Three monasteries, three communities
highlights.text: Yangang's Lepcha Monastery, Gurung Monastery and Yangang Monastery reflect the mix of people who live here. Visiting two or three of them on foot is an easy half day and a good introduction to village life.

highlights.title: Homestays in a working village
highlights.text: A small group of family homestays offers simple rooms and home food, at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with meals. Hosts farm maize, ginger and cardamom, and can show you the fields and the kitchen.

highlights.title: Ravangla and Temi within reach
highlights.text: Ravangla's Buddha Park and Maenam trailhead are about 45 minutes to an hour away, and Temi tea garden is a similar drive, so Yangang works as a quiet base for South Sikkim sightseeing.

how_to_reach.text: A few shared jeeps link Yangang with Ravangla, Namchi and Singtam each day, mostly early morning and afternoon, for about ₹100–250 a seat depending on the run. Your host will know current times. From Gangtok, a shared jeep to Ravangla costs about ₹250–400. Fares are indicative; check current status before you travel.

A reserved small car from Ravangla costs about ₹1,200–1,500 for roughly 20 km, 45 minutes to an hour. From Gangtok a car costs about ₹4,000–5,000 one way, around 3–3.5 hours via Singtam. Village roads are narrow, so allow extra time after rain.

About 120–130 km and 4.5–5 hours via NH10 and Singtam, or via Melli and Namchi, for about ₹6,000–7,500 by reserved car. When NH10 is closed by monsoon slides, drivers route through Darjeeling district and Jorethang, which adds time. Most guests break the journey in Namchi or Ravangla.

where_to_stay: Stay in Yangang itself for the village and the walks: a small group of family homestays offers simple, clean rooms and home-cooked meals at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night. Hot water may come by bucket. We match guests to homes we know and brief hosts on dietary needs beforehand. If you prefer a hotel, base yourself in Ravangla at Mt. Narsing Village Resort or The Barfung Retreat and visit Yangang for the day.
tips: Hire a local guide for anything beyond the village paths; Maenam's forest trails branch and cloud comes in quickly.
Start the Bhaleydhunga walk before dawn and turn back by early afternoon, whatever the progress.
Carry cash: Yangang has few card or UPI options and no reliable ATM for visitors.
Visit Neya Khola falls in September–October for the best flow, but take care on wet rocks.
Book homestays ahead from October to December; there are only a few rooms in the village.

experiences.title: Guided day hike towards Bhaleydhunga
experiences.summary: A long, steep day walk with a local guide from Yangang up through the forests of the Maenam ridge towards Bhaleydhunga, the rooster-shaped rock that looms over the village. For fit walkers only, in dry weather, with an early start and a firm turnaround time.
body: Bhaleydhunga, Nepali for rooster rock, is the beak-like outcrop on the Maenam ridge visible from much of South Sikkim. Reaching it on foot is a serious day: a climb of well over a thousand metres from Yangang through farmland, then oak, rhododendron and bamboo forest within or beside Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary.

The trail is not signposted and branches often, which is why a local guide is essential. Cloud can close in by late morning and paths are muddy and steep. Your guide will set a pace and a turnaround time; please respect it even if the rock seems close. Views back over the Teesta side of Sikkim reward you well before the top.

Start before dawn with a packed breakfast and lunch, at least 2 litres of water, rain gear and a warm layer. Forest department rules apply inside the sanctuary and may include fees or guide requirements; proposed ropeway and skywalk projects may also change access. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Bhaleydhunga hike?
faqs.a: Difficult. It is a long, steep, unmarked forest walk with a large height gain and a full day out, usually 8 to 10 hours. You should be a fit, experienced hill walker with good shoes. It is not suitable for children, seniors or anyone with knee or heart problems. Always go with a local guide.

faqs.q: Is there a ropeway to Bhaleydhunga?
faqs.a: A ropeway and a skywalk at Bhaleydhunga have been proposed, and the Wikipedia article on Yangang mentions them as planned projects. At the time of writing we cannot confirm that either is open to visitors. Plans like these change, so check current status before you travel and ask us.

faqs.q: What is the best season for Bhaleydhunga?
faqs.a: October and November give the most settled weather and clearest views, with March and April a good second for rhododendron in the forest. Avoid the monsoon, from June to September, when trails are slippery and leech-ridden, and deep winter, when the upper ridge is cold and can see snow.

experiences.title: A short walk to Neya Khola falls
experiences.cost: Free, or ≈ ₹300–500 for a local guide
experiences.summary: An easy outing from your homestay to Neya Khola, a forest stream and waterfall near the village listed among Yangang's natural sights. Best just after the monsoon, when the water is high and the forest green, and a good first walk on arrival.
body: Neya Khola, khola meaning stream in Nepali, drops through forest close to the village and appears in the Wikipedia article on Yangang among its local sights. It is not a famous roadside waterfall with stalls and parking, and that is the appeal: a quiet walk through fields and trees to moving water.

Your host or a neighbour can lead the way. The path passes farms of maize, ginger and cardamom before entering forest. Expect birdsong, butterflies after the monsoon and a cool, damp spot at the falls where you can sit for a while. Water levels depend on recent rain.

Go in September to November for the best flow and clear paths. In the monsoon the stream can be dangerous and leeches are common, and by late spring the falls may be thin. Wear shoes with grip, keep away from slippery rocks at the edge and do not swim in pools after rain.

faqs.q: How far is Neya Khola falls from Yangang?
faqs.a: It lies close to the village and is usually reached in under an hour on foot from most homestays, depending on where you stay. Allow about two hours for the round trip with time at the falls. Ask your host to walk you there or to point out the start.

faqs.q: When is Neya Khola falls best?
faqs.a: Just after the monsoon, from September to November, when the stream is full and the paths have dried enough to walk safely. During heavy monsoon rain the stream can be dangerous. By April and May the flow is usually much lower, though the forest walk is still pleasant.

faqs.q: Is the walk to Neya Khola safe for children?
faqs.a: Yes, for children used to walking, with an adult close by. The path is mostly gentle, but rocks near the falls are slippery and the water can be strong after rain. Keep children back from the edge and do not let them climb on wet rocks.

experiences.title: Lepcha, Gurung and Yangang monasteries on foot
experiences.summary: A half-day walk linking three of Yangang's monasteries, each tied to a different community in this mixed village. A gentle introduction to how Lepcha, Gurung and Bhutia Buddhist traditions sit side by side in South Sikkim, with tea in a village home along the way.
body: Wikipedia's article on Yangang lists a Lepcha Monastery, a Gurung Monastery and Yangang Monastery among the village's sights. Each serves part of the community, and visiting them on one walk shows how varied rural Sikkim is, even within a single village.

The route follows village roads and footpaths between farms and houses, with short climbs. At each monastery, look for differences in murals, prayer flags and the people who gather there. Caretakers are not always present, so a host or local guide who knows who holds the keys makes all the difference.

Remove shoes and hats inside, walk clockwise around shrines and stupas, and ask before photographing interiors or people. A small donation is customary. Timings are informal; mornings are best. Carry water and a rain jacket, and pause for tea if a family invites you in.

faqs.q: Which monasteries are in Yangang?
faqs.a: The village has a Lepcha Monastery, a Gurung Monastery and the main Yangang Monastery, along with a Shiva shrine at Mahadev Than. They reflect the Lepcha, Gurung, Bhutia and other Nepali-speaking families who live in Yangang. Your homestay host can plan a walking route between them.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for the monastery walk?
faqs.a: It helps a lot. Village paths are not signposted, and monasteries are sometimes locked unless a caretaker is found. A host or local guide, about ₹300–600 per group indicative, can open doors, explain the murals and introduce you to people along the way.

faqs.q: What should we wear to visit monasteries?
faqs.a: Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees, and shoes that are easy to remove, since you take them off before entering. Carry socks for cold floors in winter. Remove hats inside and keep your voice low. There is no strict dress code, but respectful dress is appreciated.

experiences.title: Ginger, maize and a Yangang homestay table
experiences.best_time: October to December for harvest; any month for the kitchen
experiences.summary: Walk your hosts' fields of ginger, maize and vegetables, then help in the kitchen as the family cooks dinner from what they grow. A simple, honest way to understand village life and to taste Sikkimese home food rather than hotel menus.
body: Yangang's slopes grow maize, ginger, cardamom and vegetables, and most homestay hosts still farm. Ask to walk the fields in the morning: depending on the season you may see ginger being lifted and washed in late autumn, maize hung to dry under the eaves, or spring planting on fresh terraces.

In the afternoon, join the kitchen. Dinner is usually rice, dal, a curry and seasonal greens such as squash shoots, nettle or fiddlehead fern, with pickles and sometimes gundruk, fermented leafy greens. Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali households each have their own dishes; ask what is special in yours.

Tell your hosts about any dietary needs when you book. Wash hands first and follow their lead in the kitchen. Wear old shoes in the fields, carry water, and remember the household works to its own rhythm: this is joining in, not a cooking class.

faqs.q: What food do Yangang homestays serve?
faqs.a: Home cooking: rice, dal, vegetable or meat curry, seasonal greens, pickles and sometimes gundruk or local cheese. Breakfast may be roti, puri or sel roti with potato curry. Meals are usually included in the homestay rate of about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night, indicative.

faqs.q: When is ginger harvested in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Ginger is generally lifted from about November into the winter, varying with altitude and the season's weather. Maize is harvested in late summer and early autumn. Ask your hosts what will be happening in the fields during your stay, since every family's calendar differs slightly.

faqs.q: Can vegetarians stay in Yangang homestays?
faqs.a: Yes, easily. Everyday meals are largely vegetarian, and meat is simple to leave out. Tell your hosts when you book if you are vegetarian or vegan, or avoid egg, onion or garlic, so they can plan the household meal around your needs.

faqs.q: Is Yangang worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you enjoy walking and village life. Yangang offers homestays in a working farm village, three monasteries of different communities, Neya Khola falls and the long hike towards Bhaleydhunga. It has few formal sights and little nightlife. Two nights, with Ravangla or Temi nearby, is the right pace.

faqs.q: How far is Yangang from Ravangla?
faqs.a: About 20 km, roughly 45 minutes to an hour by car on narrow village roads. A reserved small car costs about ₹1,200–1,500 one way. A few shared jeeps run each day for less. Fares are indicative; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is Bhaleydhunga?
faqs.a: Bhaleydhunga is a large rock outcrop on the Maenam ridge above Yangang. Its Nepali name means rooster rock, for its beak-like shape. It is visible from much of South Sikkim and can be approached on a long, steep guided day hike from the village. A ropeway and skywalk have been proposed.

faqs.q: How do we get to Yangang from Gangtok?
faqs.a: By road, about 70–80 km and 3–3.5 hours depending on the route, via Singtam or via Ravangla. A reserved small car costs about ₹4,000–5,000 one way. On a budget, take a shared jeep to Ravangla and change to a local jeep or taxi.

faqs.q: Where can we stay in Yangang?
faqs.a: In a small group of family homestays, at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with meals. Rooms are simple and clean; hot water may be by bucket. There are no large hotels. For more comfort, stay in Ravangla and visit Yangang as a day trip.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Yangang?
faqs.a: October to December for clear skies and harvest season, and March to May for warm days and forest flowers. Winter days are sunny but nights cold. June to September is the monsoon, with heavy rain, leeches and slippery trails, so long walks are best avoided then.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Yangang?
faqs.a: Indians do not need a permit. Foreign nationals need the standard Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, applied online through the e-FRRO portal since January 2026. Forest department rules and fees may apply on Maenam sanctuary trails. Homestays collect the ₹50 state entry fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Yangang good for families?
faqs.a: Yes, for families who enjoy simple stays. The village is safe and quiet, altitude is moderate at about 1,500 m, and short walks to Neya Khola falls and the monasteries suit children. Leave the Bhaleydhunga hike to fit adults. Medical care is in Ravangla, Namchi or Singtam.

faqs.q: Is Yangang connected to Pawan Chamling?
faqs.a: Yes. Yangang is the birthplace of Pawan Kumar Chamling, who served as Chief Minister of Sikkim from 1994 to 2019. The village is also the chosen site of Sikkim University's campus and has the state's main police training centre, according to Wikipedia's article on Yangang.
